title: Billing disputes with motor carriers: 180-day window to contest
summary: A shipper that wants to contest a motor carrier's original bill, or to seek more charges, must do so within 180 days of receiving the bill. This sets the auditor's default deadline for LTL and truckload overcharge disputes.
keyPoints: 180 days from receipt of the original bill.
Applies to motor carriers subject to Title 49, Part B jurisdiction.
Carrier and shipper may waive rights by written contract (49 U.S.C. § 14101(b)); check the transportation agreement.
sourceAuthority: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives

title: Limitation on actions by and against carriers (overcharges)
summary: Sets the statute of limitations for court actions over freight charges: generally 18 months for carriers to collect charges and for shippers to recover overcharges, with extensions when a claim was filed in writing.
keyPoints: Shipper actions to recover overcharges: generally within 18 months after the claim accrues.
Different from the 180-day billing dispute window in § 13710; both can apply.
sourceAuthority: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives

title: Carmack Amendment: carrier liability for loss and damage
summary: Motor carriers are liable for actual loss or injury to property they transport. Carriers may not set a claim-filing period shorter than 9 months, or a lawsuit period shorter than 2 years from written denial.
keyPoints: Claim filing period may not be shorter than 9 months.
Civil action period may not be shorter than 2 years from the carrier's written disallowance.
Liability can be limited by released rates agreed in writing.
sourceAuthority: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives

title: Principles and practices for investigating and voluntary disposition of loss and damage claims
summary: How motor carriers must handle written loss and damage claims: what a claim must contain, acknowledgment within 30 days, and payment, declination or a settlement offer within 120 days (with status updates after that).
keyPoints: A claim must identify the shipment, assert liability, and demand a specified or determinable amount (§ 370.3).
Carrier acknowledges within 30 days (§ 370.5).
Carrier pays, declines, or offers a settlement within 120 days, or reports status every 60 days after (§ 370.9).

title: Weekly retail on-highway diesel prices (fuel surcharge index)
citation: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Gasoline and Diesel Fuel Update
summary: The weekly diesel price most carrier fuel-surcharge tables are indexed to. The auditor compares each bill's fuel surcharge to the contract table at the ship-week price, so the intake package should record this price for each ship date.
keyPoints: Published weekly, national and regional (PADD) averages.
Confirm which region and which publication day the carrier contract uses.

title: Hazmat employee training requirements
summary: Every hazmat employee (including warehouse staff who prepare, load or handle hazmat shipments) needs general awareness, function-specific, safety and security training, with recurrent training at least once every three years and records kept.
keyPoints: Recurrent training at least once every three years (§ 172.704(c)(2)).
Training records kept for each hazmat employee (§ 172.704(d)).

title: Powered industrial trucks: operator training and evaluation
summary: Forklift and other powered industrial truck operators must be trained and evaluated before operating, and evaluated at least once every three years. The employer certifies training. State-plan states enforce an equivalent or stricter rule.
keyPoints: Performance evaluation at least once every three years (§ 1910.178(l)(4)(iii)).
Employer certification of training and evaluation (§ 1910.178(l)(6)).

title: Portable fire extinguishers: inspection and annual maintenance
summary: Portable extinguishers must be inspected monthly and get a maintenance check at least once a year, with records kept. The auditor treats the annual maintenance record as a credential with an expiry date.
keyPoints: Visual inspection monthly (§ 1910.157(e)(2)).
Annual maintenance check, recorded (§ 1910.157(e)(3)).

title: Handling materials: general (storage, aisles, stacking)
summary: General requirements for warehouse material storage: clearances where mechanical handling equipment is used, aisles kept clear and marked, and storage stacked and secured so it can't slide or collapse.

title: Recording and reporting occupational injuries and illnesses
summary: OSHA injury and illness recordkeeping (Forms 300, 300A, 301). Ask the 3PL for its 300A summary as part of vendor due diligence. Electronic submission rules depend on establishment size and industry.

title: OSHA-approved State Plans
summary: Lists the states that run their own OSHA-approved workplace safety programs. In those states the state agency enforces rules at least as effective as federal OSHA, and sometimes stricter.

title: FDA food facility registration
summary: Facilities that manufacture, process, pack or hold food for U.S. consumption, including third-party warehouses, must register with FDA and renew every two years (October through December of even-numbered years).
keyPoints: Holding food (storage) counts; most third-party food warehouses must register.
Biennial renewal in the Oct–Dec window of each even-numbered year.

title: Storage of unexposed packaged food (modified preventive controls)
summary: Warehouses that only store packaged food not exposed to the environment follow modified requirements, chiefly temperature controls, monitoring and records for refrigerated food that needs them for safety.

title: Sanitary transportation of human and animal food
summary: Requirements for shippers, loaders, carriers and receivers of food moved by motor or rail vehicle: vehicle condition, temperature control, training, and written procedures. The 3PL is often the 'loader' or 'shipper' under this rule.

title: DSCSA: national standards for third-party logistics providers
summary: Third-party logistics providers handling prescription drugs must be licensed, by the state they operate from or, where the state doesn't license 3PLs, by FDA, and must report licensure to FDA annually.
keyPoints: Licensure by the state where the 3PL facility is located, or by FDA where the state has no program.
Annual report to FDA.
sourceAuthority: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives

title: DEA registration of manufacturers, distributors and dispensers of controlled substances
summary: Facilities that store or distribute controlled substances need DEA registration and must meet physical security requirements (vaults, cages, alarm systems) for the schedules they handle.
